newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia makes offer to Serbs in last enclave.
newsitem.headline: Croatia makes offer to Serbs in last enclave.

text.p: Croatia said on Saturday it had offered concessions to Serbs in the country's last breakaway enclave to smooth the area's return to Zagreb's rule, including possible exemption from military service.

The state-run daily Vjesnik said the government had drafted a "Memorandum on the Completion of Peaceful Reintegration" of Eastern Slavonia and handed it to Jacques Klein, head of the U.N. Transitional Authority (UNTAES) in the region, last week.
UNTAES, backed by 5,000 multinational troops, is overseeing the gradual reinstatement of Croatian state institutions in Eastern Slavonia, due to be completed by mid-1997.

Vjesnik said the memorandum offered the Serbs several senior posts in the government and the possibility of Serb men being spared the compulsory one-year draft into the Croatian army on the basis of "objections of conscience".

Ivica Vrkic, the government official in charge of Eastern Slavonia's reintegration, said Serbs who had not lived there in 1991 but once inhabited another part of Croatia would be able to vote in Eastern Slavonia if they chose.

About half the estimated 120,000 Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, a fertile region skirting the Danube River border with Serbia, are war refugees from former Serb rebel enclaves further west in Croatia which were recaptured by government troops in 1995.
The Croatian government hitherto had guaranteed only pre-war Serb residents of Eastern Slavonia the right to vote in countrywide local elections scheduled for March 16.
The memorandum appeared to meet most demands local Serb leaders put forward in preliminary meetings with President Franjo Tudjman and other government aides.

UNTAES, Croatian and Serb officials have completed a census of Eastern Slavonia to determine who is eligible to vote in March, when Serbs involved in the 1991 revolt against Croatian independence will take part in a Croatian election for the first time since.
Rebel Krajina Serbs captured almost a third of Croatia after it seceded from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia.
Up to 200,000 Serbs fled Croatian government army offensives over U.N. ceasefire lines in 1995. The majority ended up in Serbia or Serb-held Bosnia.
Croatia's nationalist government has been severely criticized by the West over violence against mostly elderly Serbs remaining in the recaptured regions and for hindering the return of refugees.
A leading Serbian government-controlled daily, Politika, said on Saturday the memorandum represented a step towards a smooth reintegration of Eastern Slavonia.
"This (Memorandum) gives the Serbs a chance to choose if they want to vote in their current place of living or in the towns where they lived before the war," Vrkic told Vjesnik.
But he said it did not mean Croatia would allow all Serbs to remain in Eastern Slavonia, to which some 80,000 Croatian refugees expelled in 1991 are anxious to return.
"Only those who can handle their housing problem on their own (can stay). No Serb will be allowed to live in a Croatian house," Vrkic said.
